cd.t: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal

items.tx:
We just learned more about Trump’s Venezuela oil deal, and here’s everything you need to know:

1. This deal is structured to hide the identities of people who stand to profit from it.

You don’t hide that unless you have a reason to. And the man whose firm Trump just bought a 35% stake in? Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan billionaire who has faced several money-laundering investigations around the world.

2. Don’t expect cheaper gas anytime soon. 

Experts have been telling us for MONTHS that oil production in Venezuela isn’t going to lower U.S. gas prices anytime soon. Betancourt’s company is able to deliver as much oil in a year as the U.S. uses in a few days. Anyone promising this deal will bring down prices at the pump is selling you lies. 

3. If there’s a legal fight over this agreement, it has to go through a Texas court that Trump’s DOJ has repeatedly turned to for favorable rulings.

4. This deal creates a board designed to be shielded from oversight and accountability. Trump’s own Treasury Secretary wasn’t able to give Congress basic answers or audits when he testified about Venezuela just last month. But we should blindly trust them now?

So let’s recap: Americans aren’t going to feel relief at the pump. The identity of the people involved is conveniently hidden from us. And legal disputes go to a specific court that disproportionately rules in Trump’s favor.

Whatever you think American foreign policy towards Venezuela should be, Congress and the public deserve to know who’s involved and where the money is going.

cd.t: Bibi Hasn’t Won But the Opposition Has Lost

items.tx:
Last night, the exit polls told one story: Netanyahu had lost, but it wasn’t clear who on the other side had won. This morning, the results are telling another. Netanyahu hasn’t won yet, but the change bloc has clearly lost.

I’ve covered politics since the start of the century. I have never seen a camp organize for an election as impeccably, as efficiently and as energetically as the change bloc did. It signed model surplus-vote agreements, so that no leftover votes would go to waste, and ran an unprecedented operation flying Israelis home from abroad to vote. And by the actual count, it ended up with more or less the same number of seats as in the last election.

Demography beat energy, and the message also proved flawed and unsuccessful. The public wasn’t convinced that the war had been a total victory, as Netanyahu claimed, but it also refused to buy the opposition’s claim that it was a total failure. It was repelled by Haredi draft-dodging, but didn’t think the solution was a minority government propped up by draft refusers and anti-Zionists. It was disgusted when ultra-Orthodox protesters chanted “We do not believe in the rule of the Zionists,” but it was just as shocked when “Biladi, Biladi,” the Palestinian national anthem, was sung at the Joint List’s headquarters last night.

Netanyahu’s position changed completely between the release of the exit polls and the arrival of the real results. Last night it seemed clear that Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Likud loyalist, would be ousted and that, one way or another, Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff, would form a minority government. Now, by the criteria Eisenkot himself set, he has lost the legitimacy to form such a government. He promised he wouldn’t rely on the Arab parties’ votes, yet without a majority he would now need the active support of the Joint List, which looks futile and pointless. In post-October 7 Israel, there is no chance that a coalition including six candidates who lost immediate family to Hamas could last long alongside Joint List lawmakers who claim Hamas is simply a charitable organization.

After the 1967 war, Defense Minister Moshe Dayan famously said Israel was waiting for the Arabs to call. In the same spirit, Netanyahu in effect told the change camp before dawn: here’s my phone number, feel free to use it. Yisrael Beiteinu’s Avigdor Lieberman, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Eisenkot now face a dilemma from hell. They can go to another election, one that Israelis abroad will no longer fly home for. They can try to join Netanyahu’s bloc on tough terms, breaking their campaign pledges never to sit with him. Or they can beg the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List, now drunk on their success, for support.

And one final note: for the entire campaign, we searched for a third bloc, a centrist unity bloc between Netanyahu and his rivals. Candidates included Benny Gantz and former UN Ambassador Gilad Erdan, former general Ofer Winter and economist Yaron Zelekha, former Culture Minister Hili Tropper and who even remembers who else. They all collapsed, evaporated or vanished. And now it turns out the unity bloc may have been the Arab parties all along. Their historic, almost hysterical turnout, at rates that will need careful examination, shattered both sides’ dreams of a 61-seat majority. It reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all.

items.tx:
💡MOSSADIL COMMENTARY:
THE ARROGANCE OF THE ANTI-BIBI MOVEMENT

There is a lesson from this election that goes far beyond Benjamin Netanyahu.

For years, a large part of Israel’s opposition has built its political identity around one central objective: Bibi must go.

That may be an effective slogan. It is not a governing philosophy.

You cannot build an entire political movement around opposition to one man, spend an election telling voters primarily who they should reject, and then be surprised when millions of Israelis ask a very basic question:

What exactly are you offering instead?

That is where I believe the arrogance of the anti-Bibi movement became its greatest political weakness.

It operated as though opposition to Netanyahu was itself enough to create a majority. As though the public’s concerns about security, Jewish identity, Iran, Judea & Samaria, the Palestinians and the future character of the state were secondary to the question of Netanyahu’s personality.

But elections have a way of exposing political echo chambers.

The counting is still underway, and the final coalition picture remains unresolved. Early results and exit polls have shown neither major bloc comfortably reaching the 61 seats required to govern on its own.

Whatever the final numbers are, the political choices made after this election may matter almost as much as the results themselves.

Because Netanyahu’s opponents now face a decision that voters will remember.

Do they attempt to build a broad Zionist government with people they profoundly disagree with politically?

Or does removing Netanyahu remain such an overriding objective that they would rather depend on parties outside the Zionist political consensus?

That question became impossible to ignore last night.

At Joint List headquarters, supporters were filmed singing “Biladi, Biladi,” the Palestinian national anthem.

People can interpret that scene however they choose. But politically, opposition leaders should understand exactly how it will be viewed by a very large portion of the Israeli public.

These are Israelis who serve in the IDF, send their children to reserve duty, bury friends and relatives, live through rockets and wars, and may disagree fiercely with Netanyahu.

Many of them are not ideological Likud voters.

Some are centrists. Some are traditional Labor voters. Some desperately want new leadership.

But asking those voters to accept a government whose survival depends on parties whose supporters celebrate an election result by singing the Palestinian national anthem is not a minor political detail.

It is a decision that will have to be defended.

And there is now another issue hanging over the election.

Police arrested three suspects in the Negev on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters to support Ra’am. Investigators say they discovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Ra’am ballot slips.

That does not prove that Arab turnout was fraudulent. It does not prove a nationwide conspiracy. It certainly does not justify declaring the election stolen before investigators establish the facts.

But it is serious.

And every credible allegation should be investigated completely, wherever it leads.

What opposition leaders do now will therefore be watched extremely closely.

For nearly a decade, the ruling class operated under the arrogant assumption that sovereign power existed solely to protect them and punish you.

Consider the spectacle unfolding in federal courtrooms across this country. James Comey, the towering figurehead of bureaucratic narcissism who treated the director’s chair at the FBI as his personal pulpit, now sits exposed before the law, trapped under the weight of criminal indictments for unauthorized disclosures and congressional deception. The man who demanded absolute reverence from the public proved incapable of adhering to the basic statutes he spent a career wielding against his enemies.

Beside him in the dock stand the architects of the Foreign Influence Task Force. These ex-FBI officials spent years lecturing the nation about Russian subversion while actively conspiring to bury the Hunter Biden laptop and subsequently lying to congressional investigators under oath. They coordinated suppression campaigns, misled lawmakers, and abused their clearances to safeguard their preferred political dynasty. The stench of their deception is now documented on official criminal dockets.

Turn your gaze to the halls of Congress, where Eric Swalwell remains the living emblem of institutional decay. An elected representative compromised by an operative of the Chinese Communist Party was never expelled or held to account by his party; he was elevated, shielded, and paraded as a defender of national security. They demand that American citizens surrender their earnings, obey every administrative diktat, and accept stagnant wages, while criminal cartels and foreign nationals breach sovereign borders with complete impunity. They despise the working citizens who fund this nation, and they intend to disarm the agencies that protect them.
